title: Independent and Dependent Variables: Examples | AnswerThis
summary: The independent variable is what you change or compare. The dependent variable is what you measure. See 20 research examples, plus control variables.
body_markdown:
Independent and dependent variables are the two halves of the relationship a study tests: the independent variable is what you change or compare, and the dependent variable is what you measure to see whether it responds. For example, if you test whether sleep loss slows reaction time, hours of sleep is the independent variable and reaction time is the dependent variable. In a drug trial, the treatment is the independent variable and blood pressure might be the dependent variable.


Below are a quick test for telling them apart, 20 research examples from seven fields, the other variables to know, and how to turn your variables into a research question and hypothesis.


## TL;DR


-


The independent variable is what you change or compare. The dependent variable is what you measure.


-


If “the effect of X on Y” makes sense, X is the independent variable. It goes on the horizontal axis of a graph.


-


Control and confounding variables are the other factors that could explain your result.


-


Only an experiment, where you assign the independent variable, can show cause and effect on its own.


## What is the difference between independent and dependent variables?


Here is the difference in two sentences. The independent variable is what you change or compare, such as a teaching method, a drug dose or a group of people. The dependent variable is what you measure to see whether it changes, such as test scores, blood pressure or sales.


The open textbook[Research Methods in Psychology](https://kpu.pressbooks.pub/psychmethods4e/chapter/experiment-basics/) defines the independent variable as the one the experimenter manipulates and the dependent variable as the one the experimenter measures, “the presumed effect.” The[National Library of Medicine](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/oet/ed/stats/02-200.html) puts it in health terms: the independent variable is what you expect will influence the dependent variable, and the dependent variable is what happens as a result.


The name is the clue. The dependent variable depends on the independent one. The different values of the independent variable, such as 4 or 8 hours of sleep, are called its levels or conditions.


## How do you tell which is which?


Three quick tests settle most cases:


-


The “effect of” test. Fill in “the effect of ___ on ___.” Whatever fits the first blank is the independent variable. “The effect of sleep on reaction time” makes sense. “The effect of reaction time on sleep” does not.


-


The “depends on” test. Say “\[dependent\] depends on \[independent\].” Reaction time can depend on sleep.


-


The time test. The independent variable comes first. It is set, or already in place, before the outcome you measure.


In an observational study, the same tests tell you the roles, but write “association” in your paper rather than “effect.”


On a graph, the independent variable conventionally goes on the x-axis (horizontal) and the dependent variable on the y-axis (vertical). If your graph looks backwards, check whether you swapped them.

## What other variables should you know?


Your methods section will likely mention some of these:


-


Control variable: something you hold constant so it cannot explain your result, such as testing every participant in the same room.


-


Extraneous variable: any variable other than your independent and dependent variables, such as room temperature or a participant’s mood.


-


Confounding variable: an extraneous variable linked to both the independent and dependent variables, so it offers another explanation. In the National Library of Medicine’s example, nearby factory pollution could confound a link between vehicle exhaust and childhood asthma.


-


Moderator: changes the strength or direction of the relationship. If exercise lowers anxiety more in older adults than in younger ones, age is a moderator.


-


Mediator: explains how or why the relationship happens. If exercise improves sleep and better sleep lowers anxiety, sleep is a mediator.


Both definitions follow[Baron and Kenny (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173) , the classic paper on the distinction.


## How do variables work in experiments and observational studies?


In an experiment, you assign the independent variable, ideally at random, and hold other factors constant. Research Methods in Psychology calls these two features manipulation and control. Together they let you say the independent variable caused the change.


In an observational study, you measure both variables as they already are. You might record how many hours students spend on social media and their depression scores. Since nobody assigned anything, many researchers call the variables the predictor and the outcome.


An observational study alone does not show cause, for two reasons that book’s[chapter on correlational research](https://kpu.pressbooks.pub/psychmethods4e/chapter/correlational-research/) explains. The direction may run the other way: students with more depressive symptoms may use social media more. Or a third variable, such as loneliness, may drive both. Measuring likely third variables and[controlling for them statistically](https://kpu.pressbooks.pub/psychmethods4e/chapter/complex-correlation/) helps, but it cannot rule out the ones you did not measure.


Observational designs still matter, and are sometimes the only ethical option. You cannot assign people to smoke. For how designs fit with sampling and analysis choices, see our[research methodology examples](https://answerthis.io/blog/research-methodology-examples-practical-guide) .


## How do you put the variables into a research question and a hypothesis?


Once you have named your variables, the research question nearly writes itself. Two templates cover most quantitative studies:


-


Experiment: What is the effect of \[independent variable\] on \[dependent variable\] among \[population\]?


-


Observational: Is \[predictor\] associated with \[outcome\] among \[population\]?


Then turn the question into a pair of hypotheses. Here is the heart failure study from the table:


-


Null hypothesis: There is no difference in 30-day readmission rates between adults with heart failure who receive a nurse-led discharge session and those who receive standard discharge.


-


Alternative hypothesis: Adults with heart failure who receive a nurse-led discharge session will have a lower 30-day readmission rate than those who receive standard discharge.


Both name the independent variable (type of discharge), the dependent variable (30-day readmission) and the population. Our guide on[how to write a hypothesis](https://answerthis.io/blog/how-to-write-a-hypothesis) walks through the full process, from research question to checking your design.


For a first draft, the AnswerThis[hypothesis generator](https://answerthis.io/hypothesis-generator) drafts three null and alternative hypothesis pairs, each with variables, a population and suggested measurements. You describe the relationship, population or materials, comparison and measurement period you want to study, and it includes three successful free runs per browser. Treat the three pairs as candidates, then check each one against the literature and your design.


## What are the most common mistakes?


-


Naming a topic instead of a variable. “Stress” is a topic. “Score on the Perceived Stress Scale” is a dependent variable you can measure.


-


Confusing the variable with its levels. In a caffeine study, the independent variable is caffeine dose. “200 mg” and “placebo” are its levels.


-


Writing “effect” for an observational study. If you did not assign the independent variable, describe an association.


-


Ignoring confounders. List what else could explain your result before you collect data, then control it or measure it.


-


Measuring many outcomes without choosing a main one. Name a primary dependent variable in advance, so you are not tempted to report whichever one worked.


## FAQs


### Can a study have more than one independent or dependent variable?


Yes. A factorial experiment tests two or more independent variables at once, such as dose and timing, and many studies measure several outcomes.


### Can age or gender be an independent variable?


Yes, as a predictor or grouping variable. Because you cannot assign it, a study comparing groups by age or gender can show differences, but not on its own that age or gender caused them.


### What is the difference between a control variable and a control group?


A control variable is something you keep the same for everyone, such as the testing room. A control group is the group of participants who get no treatment, a placebo or usual care, which makes it one level of the independent variable.


### What are other names for independent and dependent variables?


The independent variable is also called the predictor, explanatory or exposure variable. The dependent variable is also called the outcome, response or criterion variable.


### Do qualitative studies have independent and dependent variables?


Usually not. Qualitative research explores experiences and meanings rather than measuring variables, so it is built around a phenomenon and a research question instead.
